A&P / Cardiovascular foundations

Blood flow through the heart, step by step.

The full route feels long until you split it into two loops: right heart to lungs, then left heart to body. Valves keep the sequence moving forward.

Follow the route ↓Open the free worksheet
FIELD NOTES / 003TWO CIRCUITS

Heart → lungs → heart → body → heart.

  1. 01 / PULMONARYRight heart to lungs and back
  2. 02 / SYSTEMICLeft heart to body and back

Right and left refer to the person's anatomical sides. In a front-view drawing, the person's right appears on your left.

CARDIOVASCULAR SYSTEM4 chambers4 valves2 connected circuits

01 / Trace one drop

Start where the body returns it.

After blood has delivered oxygen to body tissues, it returns to the heart with less oxygen. The right side sends it to the lungs for gas exchange. The left side receives it and pumps it into the systemic circulation.

Read the complete pathway below in order. Say each chamber and valve as you trace it; do not skip the valves just because the vessels are easier to remember.

  1. Systemic tissues → superior and inferior venae cavaeBlood returning from most of the body enters through the venae cavae. The coronary sinus also returns blood from the heart muscle to the right atrium.
  2. Right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricleThe right atrium receives venous return. Blood passes through the right atrioventricular (tricuspid) valve into the right ventricle.
  3. Right ventricle → pulmonary semilunar valve → pulmonary trunk and arteriesRight-ventricular contraction sends blood toward the lungs. The pulmonary valve lies at the exit from the right ventricle.
  4. Lung capillaries → pulmonary veins → left atriumGas exchange adds oxygen to the blood and removes carbon dioxide. Pulmonary veins carry blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
  5. Left atrium → mitral valve → left ventricleThe left atrioventricular valve is called the mitral or bicuspid valve.
  6. Left ventricle → aortic semilunar valve → aortaLeft-ventricular contraction sends blood through the aortic valve into the aorta and onward through systemic arteries.
  7. Systemic capillaries → veins → venae cavaeBlood exchanges gases and materials with tissues, then returns to the heart. The loop begins again.
THE PULMONARY CIRCUIT

Right heart → lungs

It carries blood from the right ventricle to the lung capillaries and returns it to the left atrium.

THE SYSTEMIC CIRCUIT

Left heart → body

It carries blood from the left ventricle to body tissues and returns it to the right atrium.

02 / The exam trap

Arteries go away.
Veins return.

  1. Artery

    A vessel carrying blood away from the heart. Pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood toward the lungs.

  2. Vein

    A vessel carrying blood toward the heart. Pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood from the lungs.

  3. Valve

    A one-way gate that helps prevent backflow. The name of the vessel depends on direction, not oxygen content.

03 / Retrieve the pathway

Close the page. Rebuild the route.

Try from memory first.
Then open the explanation.

Which chamber receives blood returning from the systemic circulation?

Right atrium. Most systemic venous return arrives through the superior and inferior venae cavae.

Put these in order: pulmonary veins, right ventricle, left atrium, lungs.

Right ventricle → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium. The pulmonary arteries take blood to the lungs; pulmonary veins return it to the heart.

Which valve is between the left atrium and left ventricle?

Mitral (bicuspid) valve. It is the left atrioventricular valve.

Why is the pulmonary artery a useful reminder about artery and vein names?

It is an artery because it carries blood away from the heart, even though the blood is oxygen-poor.

Memory anchor: the right side goes to the lungs; the left side goes to the body. Then insert the chambers and valves between those destinations.
